title: Gifts and Skills for God's Tent
overview: After the people's betrayal with the golden calf, Moses repeats the day of rest and invites everyone to give freely toward building the LORD's tent, and the people respond with eager generosity and skill.

parts.label: Rest comes first (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Before any building starts, Moses repeats the weekly day of rest, and even work on the sacred tent must stop for it, with death stated plainly as the penalty. Jewish tradition reads the fire rule as no kindling at all that day, while some think it mainly targeted work fires like a metalworker's forge.

parts.label: A call for willing gifts (vv. 4-9)
parts.note: Moses asks for materials to build the tabernacle, the portable tent where the LORD would be present among the people. This is not a tax: only those who are willing are asked to give.

parts.label: What the skilled will make (vv. 10-19)
parts.note: This list repeats the plans given in Exodus 25 to 31, which are now about to be carried out: the tent, the gold-covered chest called the ark, the table, lampstand, altars, basin, courtyard and the priests' clothing. Christians later read this tent as a picture of God living among people in Jesus.

parts.label: The people respond (vv. 20-29)
parts.note: Men and women alike gave what they had, from gold jewelry to yarn, goat hair and skins, while skilled women spun yarn by hand and the leaders supplied the gems, spices and oil. Much of this wealth likely came from what the Egyptians handed over when Israel left (Exodus 12:35-36), and before coins existed, jewelry often served as a family's savings.

parts.label: Bezalel and Oholiab lead (vv. 30-35)
parts.note: Moses names Bezalel of the tribe of Judah and Oholiab of the tribe of Dan to lead the work and to teach others their crafts. The text treats skill in metal, stone, wood and weaving as a gift of God's Spirit, not merely a trade.

think: What makes a gift feel truly freely given rather than expected or pressured, and does that difference matter to you?
